prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layout of a narrow outdoor work area: nearby ground and loose blocks occupy the lower foreground, low concrete walls and stacked materials lie at mid-range, and vegetation/background surfaces are farther away. Across frames 1–3, the standing person is roughly 1.5–3 m in front of the camera wearer, while the bucket/basin and wall are about 1–2 m away; by frames 4–5, the person’s torso and arm approach to within roughly 0.3–1 m, partly occluding the wall and background. Brighter regions make the nearest ground, blocks, bucket, arm, and the large object at the far right easier to separate from background surfaces than in RGB, and show the person moving from ahead/right toward the immediate foreground while turning their upper body across the view. Metric distances are uncertain because this is monocular relative depth, several surfaces merge into smooth gradients, and the black upper-right regions and object boundaries appear missing or unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map consistently isolates one standing person ahead of the camera wearer in frames 1–3, positioned near the center-right at roughly 1.5–3 m, then shows the same person expanding across the right half in frames 4–5 as they come within about 0.3–1 m. It makes the person’s occlusion of the wall and background explicit and shows a small detached person-mask fragment near the hand in frame 4, while most ground, masonry, stacked boards, bucket, and vegetation remain unlabeled and therefore cannot be spatially distinguished using this map alone. In the final frame, the person is partly out of view on the right and their arm extends toward a large near-camera object; the map labels that object as “broccoli,” but the RGB context makes this classification spatially useful only as a separate foreground region, not as a reliable object identity. The masks support left/right and overlap relationships but provide no direct depth, gaze, or facing information, and their incomplete limbs, fragmented regions, missed objects, and probable false class label make fine reach and inter-object distance estimates unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no body or hand keypoints, limb orientation, facing direction, gaze direction, reach envelope, or change in posture. It therefore cannot independently locate the visible person, distinguish the person from the camera wearer, or quantify distances and occlusions; those spatial facts are available only from the RGB and the other maps. In the RGB, the standing person moves from mid-range ahead/right into the near right foreground and becomes partly out of frame, but none of that motion is captured here. The complete absence of detections is unreliable given the clearly visible body and arm, likely reflecting failed pose estimation, severe cropping or occlusion, or insufficiently visible joints.
